---
title: "Statistics"
---


The plugin stops at description. It will count and cross-tabulate, but it will
never hand you a p-value. That is on purpose. Put a significance test in front
of most qualitative material and it invites a claim the design cannot carry,
usually because the material was never sampled in a way that would license one.

Some designs do license it, though, and for those this page exists. Note the
asymmetry: the plugin decides not to test, and you decide to. Nothing here runs
unless you call it.

## Are codes distributed independently of something?

```python
res = qdapy.chisq(frag, "citekey")
res.statistic, res.cramers_v, res.p_value
res.expected_ok
res.test
```

Read `cramers_v` first. It says how strong the association is, which is the
question you actually had; the p-value only says whether it would be surprising
under independence.

`expected_ok` is the other thing to look at. Chi-squared leans on an
approximation that falls apart once expected counts drop below about five, and
code-by-document tables get sparse quickly. When that happens the function
switches by itself. Fisher's exact test on a two-by-two table, otherwise a
Monte Carlo p-value with the margins held fixed. `res.test` says which one you
were given, and the Monte Carlo variant is seeded, so a number you publish can
be reproduced.

::: {.callout-warning title="What the unit of this test is"}

One coded fragment. Fragments from the same document are not independent
observations, so a significant result across documents is weaker evidence
than the p-value suggests. Nothing in the code can fix that for you.
:::

## Which codes travel together?

```python
d = qdapy.code_distance(frag, min_n=3)      # Jaccard distances
qdapy.mds(frag).points                      # a two-dimensional map
qdapy.gg.mds(frag)
```

Two codes are close when they sit on the same segments. `min_n` drops codes
used fewer than that many times, with two or three uses, every coefficient is
noise. `mds()` also returns `goodness`, the share of eigenvalue mass the two
dimensions carry; a map showing 30 % looks exactly like one showing 95 %.

```python
cl = qdapy.cluster(frag, min_n=3)
cl.cophenetic
cl.flat(3)
qdapy.sns.dendrogram(frag, min_n=3)
```

`cophenetic` is the correlation between the distances and the tree. Below
roughly 0.7 the dendrogram is drawing structure the distances do not support,
which is worth knowing, because a dendrogram always looks convincing. With
fewer than three codes it is undefined and reported as `nan` rather than as a
number that means nothing.

## Which codes and documents attract each other?

```python
ca = qdapy.ca(frag)
ca.inertia_share
ca.total_inertia
qdapy.gg.ca_map(frag)
```

`inertia_share` is relative to the whole table, not to the dimensions you kept
— so keeping two of four dimensions gives you something well below 1, which is
the honest answer to how much of the picture you are seeing. Shares normalised
to the retained dimensions always sum to 100 % and answer a question nobody
asked. As a sanity check, `total_inertia` equals the chi-squared statistic
divided by *n*, and the test suite verifies it.

Sources for all of the above are on the [literature page](../dev/literature.qmd).
